<<The Night Before the Century>>

Gus Atkinson stood at the boundary, his bat still humming from the day’s exertion. The crowd’s cheers had faded, but the weight of expectation lingered like a storm cloud. He had battled through the day, rescuing England from a precarious position with a display of skill and grit. Yet, as the sun dipped below the stands, the real challenge began—not the physical strain, but the mental torment of waiting. A first-class century was within reach, but first, he had to endure the longest night of his career.

The hours stretched like shadows across his hotel room. Sleep was a distant dream, interrupted by flashes of the next day’s possibilities. His stomach twisted with nerves, each passing minute amplifying the pressure. What if he failed? What if the moment slipped through his fingers? The questions gnawed at him, but Atkinson was no stranger to resilience. He had faced tougher battles, and this was just another test of his mettle.

Morning arrived, and with it, the familiar comfort of routine. He dressed, ate, and walked onto the field with a calm that belied the storm inside. The first ball came, and with a flick of his wrist, he sent it racing to the boundary. The tension dissolved with each run, replaced by the rhythm of the game. The crowd roared, but Atkinson was in his own world, a place where doubt had no place.

Chain reactions of confidence followed. A cover drive, pure and precise, took him into the 80s. A close lbw call, overturned by technology, only fueled his determination. The Sri Lankan bowlers, already weary from the previous day, offered little resistance. Atkinson seized every opportunity, his bat a blur as he carved boundaries with effortless grace. The century was no longer a distant dream but an inevitable reality.

And then, it came—a drive past mid-off, the ball racing to the boundary as if pulled by destiny. One hundred runs off one hundred balls, a perfect symmetry to his achievement. The crowd erupted, but Atkinson’s celebration was subdued, a nod to the battle he had fought within himself. As he pulled the next ball with contemptuous ease, it was clear: the night’s torment had been worth it. He had conquered not just the opposition, but the doubts that had threatened to undo him.
